title: Heidelberg to Vienna: The Oberfaktor of the Emperor
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Judengasse, house of origin
stops.campa: Into the tight lane of the Frankfurt Judengasse, walled and gated at both ends, a son is born on 21 June to the Oppenheimer line, merchants and bankers expelled once already from this city in 1612 and scattered through the Rhineland. The family is threaded across half the courts of the Reich: a brother will lead the Jews of Heidelberg and Fürth, a nephew will become the great rabbi-collector of Prague. The boy is raised inside the great commercial network of Ashkenaz, where credit travels faster than any horse.
suggested_refs: Oppenheimer family genealogy of the Court Jews

stops.name: Heidelberg, purveyor to Elector Karl Ludwig
stops.campa: Under the ruined-and-rebuilt castle on the Neckar, Samuel takes up service to Karl Ludwig, Elector Palatine, in a land bled white by the Thirty Years' War. He becomes purveyor to the elector and tax-collector of Palatine Jewry: the man who feeds an army and gathers a community's dues in the same ledger. Here he learns his craft: to advance grain, horses and coin against a prince's promise, and to make a prince's need his own security. The risky transactions begin that will one day carry him to the Kaiser's own table.
suggested_refs: The Kurpfalz under Elector Karl Ludwig

stops.name: Mannheim, the widening consortium
stops.campa: Across the Palatinate, in Mannheim, in Worms, along the Rhine trade, Samuel weaves a web of partners and agents, Jewish and Christian both, who move money and provisions between the fairs of Frankfurt and the magazines of the frontier. He is no longer a single supplier but the hub of a network. When the great war between the Kaiser and Louis XIV opens in 1673, an Austrian general marching on the Rhine notices the man who can furnish an army where the crown's own commissaries fail.
suggested_refs: The Rhine-Palatinate trade network of the Court Jews

stops.name: The Rhine front, supplier to the imperial army against France
stops.campa: The Dutch War draws the Kaiser west against Louis XIV, and along the Rhine, through Worms and the Palatine towns, Samuel assembles a consortium to victual the Austrian army in the field. This is his proving ground on the imperial stage: not a single elector's household now but the Habsburg host itself learns to depend on his wagons of grain and his advances of silver. The general who watches him work will carry his name to Vienna, and the recommendation that opens the sealed city.
suggested_refs: The Franco-Dutch War on the Rhine, 1673–1679

stops.name: Vienna, permitted through the closed gate
stops.campa: Four years after the Kaiser drove every Jew out of Vienna and razed their quarter in the Unterer Werd, the gate opens for one man. Samuel Oppenheimer is granted entry to the forbidden city and the right to bring his Gesinde, his household and a company of Jewish families, behind him. He works, from the first, for one master alone: Leopold I. He is the exception that the emptied city cannot do without, the single Jew the crown cannot afford to expel, because the crown cannot afford its own wars.
suggested_refs: The 1670 expulsion of the Jews of Vienna

stops.name: Vienna, appointed Imperial War Factor
stops.campa: On the recommendation of Margrave Ludwig of Baden, the imperial general in Hungary, to whom Samuel has advanced 100,000 gulden for the war, Leopold names him Oberfaktor and court Jew, and by 1679 imperial war factor outright. The title makes him the emperor's supplier: uniforms and bread, muskets and powder, horses for the cavalry and fodder for the horses, pay for the troops and hospitals for the wounded. By 1682 the entire commissariat of the Habsburg armies runs through his ledgers.

stops.name: Vienna, the palace on the Bauernmarkt
stops.campa: He receives what no Jew has held here in living memory: leave to build a great house in the heart of the city, at the Bauernmarkt near the Bäckerstrasse, across from a tavern. From its rooms his agents ride to every frontier; into its cellars flow the contracts and receipts of an empire's war. The mansion is the visible sign of an invisible power: the credit of one household propping up the crown of the Caesars. It is also, one day, a target.
suggested_refs: The Oppenheimer palace at Bauernmarkt, Vienna

stops.name: Vienna, the Turkish host at the walls
stops.campa: In mid-July the army of the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa, near two hundred thousand strong, closes upon Vienna and begins to dig. The emperor and his court flee up the Danube to Passau. The city is sealed, mined beneath its bastions, starving. And yet the contract Samuel signed does not lapse when the master runs: he stands to his bargain. Through the tightening ring and beyond it, his agents keep the magazines filling for the army that must be raised to break the siege.
suggested_refs: Kara Mustafa Pasha and the 1683 siege lines

stops.name: The relief army, provisioning the Entsatzheer
stops.campa: Above the besieged city the deliverance is assembled: the imperial army under Charles of Lorraine, the Poles under King Jan Sobieski, the men of the German electors. An army cannot march on courage alone. Samuel Oppenheimer takes upon himself the supply of the whole relieving host: bread and powder, remounts and fodder, coin for the soldiers, the logistics of salvation. The Court Jew, forbidden the city eleven years before, now victuals the sword that will save Christendom's gate.
suggested_refs: Jan III Sobieski, King of Poland

stops.name: The Kahlenberg, the charge that breaks the host
stops.campa: On 12 September the Christian army pours down the wooded slopes of the Kahlenberg above the Danube. In the late afternoon Sobieski leads the greatest cavalry charge the age has seen; the Ottoman line shatters, Kara Mustafa flees, and the siege is broken in a single day. The city is saved. Fed and armed by Samuel's contracts, the deliverance holds, and the Jew who could not enter Vienna has helped to keep it. Even so, this very year he and his son are briefly seized, then freed: the crown's need protects him.
suggested_refs: Sobieski's cavalry charge from the Kahlenberg
Kahlenberg and the Leopoldsberg above Vienna

stops.name: Ofen (Buda), the Danube fleet of rafts
stops.campa: The war turns from defence to conquest, driving the Ottoman back down the Danube. For the siege of Ofen, Buda, the old Hungarian crown-city held by the Turk for a century and a half, Samuel builds a whole fleet of rafts to float provisions down the river to the besiegers. On 2 September the fortress falls. Behind every imperial magazine on the Hungarian plain stands the Oberfaktor's signature; the reconquest of a kingdom rides on his credit.
suggested_refs: The 1686 siege and fall of Buda
The Danube supply fleet for the Hungarian campaign

stops.name: Philippsburg, the son taken as surety
stops.campa: War flares again on the Rhine as Louis XIV strikes east. To force faster deliveries to the imperial army at Philippsburg, the court seizes Samuel's son Emanuel and holds him as a pledge: hostage against a merchant's speed. It is the pattern of his whole life laid bare: the crown leans on him utterly, and answers his indispensability with the mailed fist. He keeps the wagons rolling; the son is loosed. The debt, meanwhile, climbs without pause.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Philippsburg on the Rhine

stops.name: Slankamen, the mounting mountain of debt
stops.campa: At Slankamen on the Danube, Ludwig of Baden smashes the Ottoman army in one of the bloodiest fields of the age, and the victory, like all the others, is fed from Samuel's stores. But the ledger tells a second story beneath the triumph. The crown's debt to him swells from 187,000 gulden in 1684 toward the millions: he advances endlessly to a treasury that pays him in privileges, promises, and suspicion. He charges his twelve per cent, his commissions, his exchange fees, and still the arrears outrun them.
suggested_refs: The Oppenheimer war-loans to the Habsburg treasury

stops.name: Zenta, the debt at three million as Eugene triumphs
stops.campa: At Zenta on the Tisza, Prince Eugene of Savoy falls upon the Ottoman army mid-crossing and annihilates it: the victory that will force the Turk to Karlowitz. Eugene's armies march on Oppenheimer's provisions; it is the Oberfaktor who arranges even their field hospitals and medicine. Yet as the greatest of imperial victories is won on his supply, the crown's debt to him has climbed past three million florins, and the treasury under his enemies plots how never to pay it. Triumph abroad, strangulation at home: the two halves of his life meet on this field.

stops.name: Vienna, Bishop Kollonitsch and the fabricated murder
stops.campa: Bishop Leopold Kollonitsch, raised to head the imperial treasury, sets himself to break the court's dependence on the Jew. He levels a charge as monstrous as it is groundless: that Samuel has plotted the murder of his own kinsman and cashier, Samson Wertheimer. Oppenheimer and his household are arrested and cast into prison as defrauders of the state. The accusation is a court intrigue dressed as a crime: the enemies within striking at the man the enemies without could not.
suggested_refs: Samson Wertheimer, court factor and kinsman

stops.name: Vienna, ransomed from prison
stops.campa: The investigation proves the charges empty, but the crown does not free him for justice's sake. He buys his own liberty: 500,000 florins to the treasury, and a fresh half-million in credit besides, before the doors open. He walks out poorer and more indispensable than ever, the debt owed to him now standing near three million florins. The lesson is bitter and plain: to serve the Caesar is to be squeezed by him, and to be needed is no shield at all.

stops.name: Vienna, Rossau: the cemetery wall and the hospital
stops.campa: Restored to favour, Samuel turns his wealth to his people. In the Rossau, along the Seegasse, he buys the old burial ground and rebuilds in stone the wall the Turks tore down in the siege of 1683. Two years on he raises beside it the first Jewish hospital and a house of care for the poor. Across the Reich he is a benefactor without precedent, endowing synagogues and yeshivot from his war-profits: the Oberfaktor building, quietly, a Jewish world in the city that had cast the Jews out.

stops.name: Karlowitz, the peace that starves the profit
stops.campa: At Karlowitz the long Turkish war ends; the Ottoman yields Hungary and Transylvania to the Kaiser. For the Oberfaktor peace is a double edge. The great flow of war-contracts slows, yet the crown's debt to him remains: colossal, unpaid, and now harder than ever to collect from a treasury no longer terrified into borrowing. The disbanded, unpaid soldiers and invalids of the war look for someone to blame, and the richest Jew in Vienna, in his palace by the Bauernmarkt, is easy to find.

stops.name: Vienna, Bauernmarkt: the mob sacks the house
stops.campa: It begins small and turns to fury. Two chimney-sweep apprentices at play outside the tavern are mocked from Oppenheimer's house; they answer with the old Jew-baiting gesture, rapping their knuckles on a bench. When Samuel calls the watch, a crowd gathers, stones and eggs fly, and the mob storms the palace, ransacking, wrecking, hurling the great ledgers of the empire's war into the street. The household flees to a cellar vault. The city guard stands idle; only the castle guard fires at last into the crowd, killing and wounding twelve.
suggested_refs: The scattered war-ledgers of the imperial commissariat

stops.name: Vienna, Petersplatz: the cannon and the gallows
stops.campa: That night the authorities wheel cannon onto the Petersplatz to overawe the city and prevent another rising. At dawn the ringleaders, a chimney-sweep and a sword-polisher, are hanged from the iron grating above the door of the very house they plundered, a warning left swinging over the wreck. Those who carried off the emperor's documents are promised amnesty if they return them swiftly, for the crown needs its ledgers back as badly as the Oberfaktor does. Order is restored; the man is not.
suggested_refs: The hanging over the plundered house

segments.name: The Debt That Outlives the Man

stops.name: Vienna, chief war factor for a new war
stops.campa: The War of the Spanish Succession opens, and the aged Oberfaktor is drawn back to the yoke, raised now to chief war factor, he and his two sons running the commissariat of the imperial armies across many fronts at once. His agents even shift the subsidy of half a million florins that buys the Saxon elector the crown of Poland. Old, plundered, owed millions, distrusted by the court he keeps solvent, he is still the one hand that can conjure an army's bread out of nothing.
suggested_refs: The War of the Spanish Succession

stops.name: Vienna, death of the Oberfaktor
stops.campa: On 3 May 1703, in the city he had fed through siege and war, Samuel Oppenheimer dies at seventy-two: the most important creditor the Habsburg state has ever had, the crown owing him millions it never means to pay. He is carried to the Rossau, to the burial ground he himself walled in stone, and laid among his people in the Seegasse. The single indispensable Jew is gone; and the empire he propped up on his own credit feels the ground shift beneath it.
suggested_refs: Samuel Oppenheimer's grave, Seegasse cemetery, Vienna
The Oberfaktor as the empire's greatest creditor

stops.name: Vienna, the Oppenheimer bankruptcy
stops.campa: The crown seizes its escape. Rather than honour its debt, the state refuses the heir Emanuel his six million florins, declares the firm bankrupt, and turns the accusation round, demanding four million from him instead, on the ancient pretext that the fortune was fraud from the start. The whole edifice of personal credit, built on trust alone, buckles at once; the exchanges linked to Oppenheimer, above all Frankfurt, plunge into crisis. His death nearly drags the empire down with it.

stops.name: Vienna, the Banco del Giro rises from the ruin
stops.campa: To catch a state falling through the hole one man's death has torn, Austria founds in 1703 its first public bank, the Banco del Giro. Where credit had rested on the trust of a single household, it must now rest on an institution. The Oberfaktor's method is nationalised over his open grave: the personal genius of the Court Jew becomes the impersonal machinery of state finance: the very thing that will make men like him, in time, no longer indispensable.
suggested_refs: The Banco del Giro (Wiener Stadtbank), founded 1703
The birth of Austrian state banking

segments.name: The Mirror of the Court Jew

stops.name: Prague, David Oppenheimer and the great library
stops.campa: In Prague sits Samuel's nephew, David Oppenheimer, chief rabbi and the age's greatest collector of Hebrew books. Prince Eugene of Savoy carries back from the Turkish wars a trove of manuscripts and lays them, through the Oberfaktor's hand, into that library: thousands of volumes that will one day cross to Oxford and rest in the Bodleian. The uncle's war-gold and the nephew's scholarship are one enterprise: the Court Jew builds not only armies' bread but the memory of a people in ink.
suggested_refs: The David Oppenheimer Collection, Bodleian Library, Oxford
David Oppenheim, chief rabbi of Prague

stops.name: Heidelberg, the birth of Joseph Süss, the mirror to come
stops.campa: Back in Heidelberg, where Samuel's own career began, a boy is born into the wider Oppenheimer kin to a Jewish tax-collector and his wife: Joseph Süss Oppenheimer, 'Jud Süss.' He will become court Jew to the Duke of Württemberg and climb as high as Samuel and higher, and then fall as Samuel never quite did: seized on his patron's death, tried, and hanged in an iron cage over Stuttgart in 1738. The same arc bends through the family twice: the indispensable financier, the enemies at court, the reckoning. In Vienna the debt was buried with the man; in Stuttgart the man was hung up as the debt.
